# Discrete-event simulation {#sec-discrete-event-simulation}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Self-study**: not taught at the workshop, but complete and ready to use on your own.
:::

The jump-process chapter simulates a continuous-time Markov chain by
tracking *aggregate counts* and repeatedly asking "what happens next, and to
how many people?" The agent-based model chapter tracks *individuals*, but
advances them in fixed time steps of $\Delta t = 0.1$. A discrete-event
simulation (DES) combines both ideas: it tracks individuals **and** advances
time continuously, jumping directly from one scheduled event to the next
without ever discretizing the clock. This appendix builds the same SIR
process as an event queue two different ways — with Agents.jl's current
`EventQueueABM`, and with the general-purpose process-oriented `ConcurrentSim.jl`
— and shows how naturally a DES can express things the earlier chapters
could not, including the fixed delay of @sec-delay-differential-equations.

## Learning goals

By the end of this unit you should be able to:

- classify an individual-level, continuous-time, event-queue simulation and
  contrast it with the population-level CTMC (jump-process chapter) and the
  discrete-time ABM (agent-based models chapter);
- construct an `EventQueueABM` with `AgentEvent`s whose propensities depend
  on agent state, using the current Agents.jl 7 API;
- construct an equivalent model with `ConcurrentSim.jl`'s coroutine-based
  processes, and explain when its more general process/resource abstraction
  is preferable to an agent-centric framework;
- validate a DES implementation with conservation, monotonicity of the
  one-way $S\to I\to R$ transition, and an ensemble comparison against the
  deterministic mean field; and
- recognize how an event's *timing* function, not just its propensity, can
  encode a fixed delay directly, connecting back to the method of steps.

## Model assumptions and classification

The population and rates are the usual baseline: $N=1000$, $S(0)=990$,
$I(0)=10$, $R(0)=0$, contact rate $c=10$, transmission probability $\beta =
0.05$, recovery rate $\gamma=0.25$. Each individual is in exactly one of
three states. A susceptible individual's next contact, and an infectious
individual's recovery, are each scheduled as an **event** at a specific
future time; the simulation clock jumps directly to the next scheduled
event anywhere in the population, executes it, and reschedules as needed.
There is no fixed time step anywhere in the model.

| Property | Classification |
|---|---|
| Determinism | Stochastic |
| Time | Continuous, event-driven (no fixed $\Delta t$) |
| State | Discrete (individual status) |
| Representation | Individual-level |

This is a **stochastic, continuous-time, discrete-state, individual-level**
model — the same underlying process as the jump-process chapter's CTMC, by
the superposition of independent exponential clocks, but resolved per
individual rather than by a single aggregate "what happens next" draw, and
without the agent-based model chapter's time-step discretization.

## Equations

Each susceptible individual's next contact is scheduled after an
$\mathrm{Exponential}(1/c)$ waiting time; when that contact fires, an
individual is drawn uniformly from the population, and infection occurs with
probability $\beta$ if that alter is infectious:

$$
T_\text{contact} \sim \mathrm{Exponential}(1/c), \qquad
\Pr(\text{infect} \mid \text{contact with infectious alter}) = \beta.
$$ {#eq-a03-contact}

The draw ranges over all $N$ individuals, including the one doing the sampling.
A draw that lands on itself, or on any susceptible or recovered individual,
passes without transmission. Counting those null draws is what gives the force
of infection its familiar form: a susceptible contacts an infectious individual
at rate $c \, I/N$, and each such contact infects with probability $\beta$, so
individuals leave $S$ at rate $\beta c I / N$. Both implementations below draw
partners this way, which is why the same deterministic curve describes them.

Each infectious individual's recovery fires after an independent
$\mathrm{Exponential}(1/\gamma)$ waiting time:

$$
T_\text{recovery} \sim \mathrm{Exponential}(1/\gamma).
$$ {#eq-a03-recovery}

By the memoryless property and superposition of independent Poisson
processes, the *population-level* counting process implied by
@eq-a03-contact and @eq-a03-recovery is exactly the CTMC of the jump-process
chapter; the individual-event view additionally retains *who* infected
*whom* and *when* each specific event is scheduled, which an event queue
(a priority queue ordered by event time) makes explicit.

## Julia implementation

### Primary: `Agents.jl` `EventQueueABM`

`EventQueueABM` associates each agent with one or more `AgentEvent`s. By
default `AgentEvent`'s `timing` samples an exponential waiting time
parameterized by the event's `propensity`, exactly matching
@eq-a03-contact–@eq-a03-recovery; only agents with nonzero propensity are
scheduled.

```{julia}
#| label: code-a03-setup
using Agents
using ConcurrentSim
using ResumableFunctions
using Random
using Distributions
using DataFrames
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using CairoMakie

const β = 0.05
const c = 10.0
const γ = 0.25
const N = 1000
const I0 = 10
const tf = 40.0
```

```{julia}
#| label: code-a03-eventqueue
@agent struct Person(NoSpaceAgent)
    status::Symbol
end

function transmit!(agent, model)
    alter = random_agent(model)
    if alter.status == :I && (rand(abmrng(model)) ≤ model.β)
        agent.status = :I
    end
    return nothing
end
recover!(agent, model) = (agent.status = :R)

transmit_propensity(agent, model) = agent.status == :S ? model.c : 0.0     # eq-a03-contact
recovery_propensity(agent, model) = agent.status == :I ? model.γ : 0.0    # eq-a03-recovery

transmit_event = AgentEvent(action! = transmit!, propensity = transmit_propensity)
recovery_event = AgentEvent(action! = recover!, propensity = recovery_propensity)
events = (transmit_event, recovery_event)

susceptible(x) = count(==(:S), x)
infected(x) = count(==(:I), x)
recovered(x) = count(==(:R), x)

function init_eventqueue_model(β, c, γ, N, I0, rng)
    properties = Dict(:β => β, :c => c, :γ => γ)
    model = EventQueueABM(Person, events; properties, rng)
    for i in 1:N
        status = i <= I0 ? :I : :S
        add_agent!(Person(; id = i, status = status), model)
    end
    return model
end

rng = Xoshiro(20250711)
eq_model = init_eventqueue_model(β, c, γ, N, I0, rng)
to_collect = [(:status, f) for f in (susceptible, infected, recovered)]
eq_data, _ = run!(eq_model, tf; adata = to_collect)
first(eq_data, 3)
```

### Alternative: `ConcurrentSim.jl` general-purpose processes

`ConcurrentSim.jl` (the maintained continuation of the historical `SimJulia`)
is not agent-centric: it provides coroutine-based *processes* that `timeout`
for arbitrary durations, plus general `Resource`/`Store` primitives for
queueing and contention. Where `EventQueueABM` gives you propensities and
actions, `ConcurrentSim` gives you the process itself as a Julia function —
more bookkeeping, but no requirement that the model be phrased as "agents
with events." Each individual here is a `@resumable` process that repeats
"wait for a contact, maybe get infected" until infected, then waits once
more to recover.

```{julia}
#| label: code-a03-concurrentsim
mutable struct SIRPerson
    id::Int
    status::Symbol
end

mutable struct SIRModel
    sim::Simulation
    β::Float64
    c::Float64
    γ::Float64
    ta::Vector{Float64}
    Sa::Vector{Int}
    Ia::Vector{Int}
    Ra::Vector{Int}
    people::Vector{SIRPerson}
end

function record!(m::SIRModel)
    push!(m.ta, now(m.sim))
    push!(m.Sa, count(p -> p.status == :S, m.people))
    push!(m.Ia, count(p -> p.status == :I, m.people))
    push!(m.Ra, count(p -> p.status == :R, m.people))
    return nothing
end

@resumable function live(sim::Simulation, person::SIRPerson, m::SIRModel, rng)
    while person.status == :S
        @yield timeout(sim, rand(rng, Exponential(1 / m.c)))      # eq-a03-contact
        alter = rand(rng, m.people)          # uniform over all N, person included
        if alter.status == :I && rand(rng) < m.β
            person.status = :I
            record!(m)
        end
    end
    if person.status == :I
        @yield timeout(sim, rand(rng, Exponential(1 / m.γ)))      # eq-a03-recovery
        person.status = :R
        record!(m)
    end
end

function init_concurrentsim_model(S, I, R, β, c, γ)
    sim = Simulation()
    people = SIRPerson[]
    for i in 1:S
        push!(people, SIRPerson(i, :S))
    end
    for i in 1:I
        push!(people, SIRPerson(S + i, :I))
    end
    for i in 1:R
        push!(people, SIRPerson(S + I + i, :R))
    end
    SIRModel(sim, β, c, γ, [0.0], [S], [I], [R], people)
end

cs_rng = Xoshiro(20250711)
cs_model = init_concurrentsim_model(N - I0, I0, 0, β, c, γ)
for person in cs_model.people
    @process live(cs_model.sim, person, cs_model, cs_rng)
end
run(cs_model.sim, tf)
(cs_model.Sa[end], cs_model.Ia[end], cs_model.Ra[end])
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-a03-trajectories
#| fig-cap: "Two independent discrete-event realisations of the same SIR process — Agents.jl's EventQueueABM and ConcurrentSim's process model — against the deterministic ODE mean field. The EventQueueABM curve is coarser because its adata collection samples the model once per unit time by default, while ConcurrentSim's manual bookkeeping records every individual event."
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    β, c, γ = p
    Ntot = S + I + R
    λ = β * c * I / Ntot
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - γ * I
    du[3] = γ * I
    return nothing
end
sol_ode = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, tf), (β, c, γ)), Tsit5())

fig = Figure(size = (720, 440))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time", ylabel = "infectious count",
          title = "Two discrete-event realisations vs the ODE mean field")
stairs!(ax, eq_data.time, eq_data.infected_status; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2,
        label = "I (EventQueueABM)")
stairs!(ax, cs_model.ta, cs_model.Ia; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 2,
        label = "I (ConcurrentSim)")
lines!(ax, sol_ode.t, sol_ode[2, :]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 2,
       label = "I (ODE mean field)")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

## Validation

**Conservation.** Every recorded row of both simulations must sum to $N$:

```{julia}
#| label: code-a03-check-conservation
conserved_eq = all(r -> r.susceptible_status + r.infected_status + r.recovered_status == N,
                    eachrow(eq_data))
conserved_cs = all(cs_model.Sa .+ cs_model.Ia .+ cs_model.Ra .== N)
(conserved_eq, conserved_cs)
```

**Monotonicity.** Because transitions are strictly $S \to I \to R$, the
susceptible count can only fall and the recovered count can only rise:

```{julia}
#| label: code-a03-check-monotone
mono_eq = issorted(eq_data.susceptible_status; rev = true) && issorted(eq_data.recovered_status)
mono_cs = issorted(cs_model.Sa; rev = true) && issorted(cs_model.Ra)
(mono_eq, mono_cs)
```

**Ensemble comparison with the mean field.** A small ensemble of
`EventQueueABM` runs should scatter around the deterministic prediction:

```{julia}
#| label: code-a03-check-ensemble
finals = Int[]
for seed in 1:20
    ensemble_rng = Xoshiro(seed)
    ensemble_model = init_eventqueue_model(β, c, γ, N, I0, ensemble_rng)
    ensemble_data, _ = run!(ensemble_model, tf; adata = to_collect)
    push!(finals, last(ensemble_data).recovered_status)
end
mean_final_R = sum(finals) / length(finals)
ode_final_R = sol_ode.u[end][3]
(mean_final_R, round(ode_final_R; digits = 1), abs(mean_final_R - ode_final_R) / ode_final_R < 0.1)
```

All checks pass: both implementations conserve $N$ exactly, both respect the
one-way state ordering, and the 20-run ensemble mean final size is within
10% of the deterministic prediction — consistent given the ensemble is small
and some realisations have not fully burned out by $t=40$.

## Interpretation and limitations

Both implementations encode identical dynamics, but the two frameworks make
different things easy. `EventQueueABM` handles scheduling and bookkeeping
automatically once propensities are declared, and its `adata` mechanism is
convenient — but by default it samples the model once per unit time, coarser
than the true event resolution, as the visibly "steppier" red curve in
@fig-a03-trajectories shows. `ConcurrentSim` requires writing the recording
logic by hand, but every event is available exactly when it happens, and its
general `Resource`/`Store` primitives (queues, limited capacity, priorities)
extend naturally to models that are not naturally agent-centric — a
patient-flow model with a limited number of hospital beds, for instance,
maps directly onto a `ConcurrentSim` `Resource` but has no obvious
`EventQueueABM` analogue.

Both frameworks share a structural limitation relative to the aggregated
jump-process chapter: scheduling and executing $O(N)$ individual events is
more expensive than resampling a single aggregate "what happens next," so
neither scales as well to very large populations. The specific transmission
rule used here, every susceptible polling a uniformly random alter, also costs
one event per susceptible however few individuals are infectious. A
production-oriented implementation would instead schedule new infection
attempts only from currently infectious individuals.

Finally, notice that nothing here required an exponential recovery time.
`AgentEvent`'s `timing` argument accepts any function
`timing(agent, model, propensity)`, not just the default exponential
sampler, and `ConcurrentSim`'s `timeout` accepts any waiting time, fixed or
random. A discrete-event framework can therefore encode the *exact* fixed
recovery delay of @sec-delay-differential-equations directly — Exercise 1
asks you to do exactly that — without any history function or method of
steps, because the individual retains its own infection time rather than
solving a continuous population-level state.

For the current APIs, see the
[Agents.jl EventQueueABM documentation](https://juliadynamics.github.io/Agents.jl/stable/api/#Agents.EventQueueABM)
and the
[ConcurrentSim.jl repository](https://github.com/JuliaDynamics/ConcurrentSim.jl).
Agents.jl itself is described in [@datseris2022].

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#a03-ex1}

Modify the `EventQueueABM` recovery event so that its `timing` function
returns a fixed value $\tau = 1/\gamma = 4$ instead of sampling an
exponential distribution — keep `recovery_propensity` constant and nonzero
for infectious agents, and write
`fixed_delay_timing(agent, model, propensity) = agent.status == :I ? τ : Inf`
as the event's `timing`. Run the modified model and compare its infectious
curve with the deterministic DDE of @sec-delay-differential-equations at the
same parameters. Explain why this individual-level construction reaches the
same fixed-delay assumption without a history function.

### Exercise 2 {#a03-ex2}

Extend the `ConcurrentSim` model with a `Resource` representing a limited
number of hospital beds: an infectious individual must successfully
`request` a bed before starting the recovery `timeout`, and must `release`
it on recovery. Run the model with a small number of beds (for example, 50)
and compare the infectious curve and the time individuals spend waiting for
a bed with the unconstrained model above. Explain why this kind of resource
contention has no natural equivalent in the `EventQueueABM` formulation used
in this appendix.
